claims.claim: In tor- mutants, timer gene temporal expression dynamics resembled those seen in the trunk of wild-type embryos.
claims.source: In tor- mutants (Figure 6B and G), all posterior spatial patterning of the timer genes was lost, and their temporal expression dynamics resembled those seen in the trunk of wild-type embryos.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B and 6G.

claims.claim: In tor- mutants, cad, D, and opa were all expressed to the very posterior of the embryo at the beginning of stage 5, with first cad and then D expression turning off as stage 5 progressed.
claims.source: Thus cad, D, and opa were all expressed to the very posterior of the embryo at the beginning of stage 5, with first cad and then D expression turning off as stage 5 progressed.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B and 6G.

claims.claim: In tor- mutants, the posterior domain of wg was absent.
claims.source: The posterior domain of wg was absent, and the region of segmental wg expression expanded posteriorly, as described previously (Mohler, 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B and 6G, as well as a citation to Mohler, 1995.

claims.claim: Loss of the cad tail domain in tor- and torso-like (tsl-) mutants has been described previously.
claims.source: Loss of the cad tail domain in tor- and torso-like (tsl-) mutants has also been described previously (Mlodzik and Gehring, 1987b; Schulz and Tautz, 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In tll- mutants, the posterior wg domain was absent.
claims.source: In tll- mutants (Figure 6C, D and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), the posterior wg domain was absent (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), and the cad, D, and opa domains were expanded posteriorly to abut the hkb domain, which looked similar to wild-type (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C, 6D, 6G, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, as well as a citation to Wu and Lengyel, 1998.

claims.claim: In tll- mutants, the cad, D, and opa domains were expanded posteriorly to abut the hkb domain.
claims.source: In tll- mutants (Figure 6C, D and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), the posterior wg domain was absent (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), and the cad, D, and opa domains were expanded posteriorly to abut the hkb domain, which looked similar to wild-type (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C, 6D, 6G, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: In tll- mutants, the hkb domain looked similar to wild-type.
claims.source: In tll- mutants (Figure 6C, D and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), the posterior wg domain was absent (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), and the cad, D, and opa domains were expanded posteriorly to abut the hkb domain, which looked similar to wild-type (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Normal expression of hkb in tll- mutants has been previously reported.
claims.source: Normal expression of hkb in tll- mutants has been previously reported (Brönner and Jäckle, 1991; Brönner et al., 1994; Ashyraliyev et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: A posteriorly shifted cad tail domain was transiently expressed in tll- mutants.
claims.source: A posteriorly shifted cad tail domain was transiently expressed (Figure 6C and G; Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C, 6G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The finding of a posteriorly shifted cad tail domain in tll- mutants conflicts with previous reports that the cad tail domain was either unaffected or completely absent in tll- mutants.
claims.source: This finding conflicts with previous reports that the cad tail domain was either unaffected (Reinitz and Levine, 1990) or completely absent (Mlodzik and Gehring, 1987b) in tll- mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim contrasts the current findings with previous reports.

claims.claim: In tll- mutants, a persistent posterior D domain did not emerge.
claims.source: The pattern of D expression in the trunk was abnormal (presumably caused by feedback from the segmentation genes, which are misregulated in tll- mutants; Mahoney and Lengyel, 1987; Casanova, 1990; Janssens et al., 2013), and a persistent posterior D domain did not emerge (Figure 6C; Figure 4—figure supplement 5).

claims.claim: tll- opa- double mutants showed similar patterning dynamics to tll- single mutants, except that tail-like expression of D was rescued and persisted into germband extension.
claims.source: tll- opa- double mutants showed similar patterning dynamics to tll- single mutants, except that tail-like expression of D was rescued and persisted into germband extension (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: In hkb- mutants, the wg posterior stripe became a posterior cap.
claims.source: In hkb- mutants (Figure 6E–H), the wg posterior stripe became a posterior cap (Mohler, 1995), and cad expression persisted longer than normal at the posterior pole.

claims.claim: In hkb- mutants, cad expression persisted longer than normal at the posterior pole.
claims.source: In hkb- mutants (Figure 6E–H), the wg posterior stripe became a posterior cap (Mohler, 1995), and cad expression persisted longer than normal at the posterior pole.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6E-H.

claims.source: The relative phasing of the cad, D, opa, and wg domains was preserved, but the whole terminal pattern was posteriorly shifted/expanded into territory that would normally express hkb (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: In hkb- mutants, the tll domain was smaller than normal, thereby preserving the correlation between tll levels and timer gene expression boundaries seen in wild-type embryos.
claims.source: In contrast to previous reports that tll expression is unaffected in hkb- mutants (Brönner and Jäckle, 1991; Brönner et al., 1994; Brönner and Jäckle, 1996), we found that the tll domain was smaller than normal, thereby preserving the correlation between tll levels and timer gene expression boundaries seen in wild-type embryos (Figure 6F and H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6F, 6H, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, and contrasts with previous reports.

claims.claim: In hkb- mutants, expression of tll persisted throughout stages 6 and 7, rather than fading at stage 6.
claims.source: Expression of tll persisted throughout stages 6 and 7, rather than fading at stage 6, and ectopic expression appeared at the anterior pole (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claims.claim: In hkb- mutants, ectopic tll expression appeared at the anterior pole.
claims.source: Expression of tll persisted throughout stages 6 and 7, rather than fading at stage 6, and ectopic expression appeared at the anterior pole (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: All posterior spatial patterning of the timer genes is dependent on the terminal system via tor.
claims.source: All posterior spatial patterning of the timer genes is dependent on the terminal system via tor.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the tor- mutant phenotype shown in Figure 6B and 6G.

claims.claim: Expression boundaries associated with the tail and hindgut are perturbed in tll- mutants.
claims.source: Expression boundaries associated with the tail and hindgut are perturbed in tll- mutants, while expression boundaries associated with the posterior midgut are perturbed in hkb- mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the tll- mutant phenotype shown in Figure 6C, 6D, 6G.

claims.claim: Expression boundaries associated with the posterior midgut are perturbed in hkb- mutants.
claims.source: Expression boundaries associated with the tail and hindgut are perturbed in tll- mutants, while expression boundaries associated with the posterior midgut are perturbed in hkb- mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the hkb- mutant phenotype shown in Figure 6E-H.

claims.claim: There is a concerted posterior shift of the fate map in hkb- embryos, which is attributed to the reduced size of the tll domain.
claims.source: In addition, there is a concerted posterior shift of the fate map in hkb- mutants, which we attribute to the reduced size of the tll domain.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the hkb- mutant phenotype shown in Figure 6E-H.

claims.claim: Tll strongly represses D and opa and weakly represses cad.
claims.source: Our observations from this and the previous section suggest that Tll strongly represses D and opa and weakly represses cad, while Hkb represses wg, cad, D, and opa (see Appendix 3—table 1 for detailed reasoning).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutant phenotypes shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: Hkb represses wg, cad, D, and opa.
claims.source: Our observations from this and the previous section suggest that Tll strongly represses D and opa and weakly represses cad, while Hkb represses wg, cad, D, and opa (see Appendix 3—table 1 for detailed reasoning).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutant phenotypes shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: Hkb is necessary for activation of tll at normal levels.
claims.source: Hkb is also necessary for activation of tll at normal levels (an interaction that is presumably indirect since Hkb acts as a repressor; Goldstein et al., 1999), and for timely repression of tll after stage 5.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the hkb- mutant phenotype shown in Figure 6F, 6H, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, and a citation to Goldstein et al., 1999.

claims.claim: Hkb is necessary for timely repression of tll after stage 5.
claims.source: Hkb is also necessary for activation of tll at normal levels (an interaction that is presumably indirect since Hkb acts as a repressor; Goldstein et al., 1999), and for timely repression of tll after stage 5.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the hkb- mutant phenotype shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In wild-type embryos at stage 5.4, the posterior fkh domain had a fairly sharp border, which lined up with the anterior border of the posterior wg domain and the posterior border of the cad tail domain.
claims.source: In wild-type embryos at stage 5.4, the posterior fkh domain had a fairly sharp border, which lined up with the anterior border of the posterior wg domain and the posterior border of the cad tail domain.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claims.claim: In cadm-z- mutants, fkh expression was strongly reduced.
claims.source: In cadm-z- mutants, fkh expression was strongly reduced (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), contrasting with the tll and hkb domains in these embryos, which looked normal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Wu and Lengyel, 1998; Olesnicky et al., 2006).

claims.claim: In cadm-z- mutants, the tll and hkb domains looked normal.
claims.source: In cadm-z- mutants, fkh expression was strongly reduced (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), contrasting with the tll and hkb domains in these embryos, which looked normal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Wu and Lengyel, 1998; Olesnicky et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In hkb- mutants, the fkh domain was reduced in size.
claims.source: In hkb- mutants, the fkh domain was reduced in size (Weigel et al., 1990; Gaul and Weigel, 1990), correlating with the reduced size of the tll domain and the posteriorly shifted wg and cad borders in this genotype.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A, 7B, and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The fkh domain was also reduced in tll- mutants.
claims.source: The fkh domain was also reduced in tll- mutants (Weigel et al., 1990; Gaul and Weigel, 1990).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A, 7B, and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In tll- mutants, the reduced fkh domain was the same size as the hkb domain, and it abutted the posteriorly shifted cad tail domain.

claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claims.claim: In fkh- mutants, the posterior wg domain was largely absent.

claims.claim: In fkh- mutants, cad, D, and opa expression was essentially normal throughout stage 5.

claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The findings on cad expression in fkh- mutants contrast with a previous report, which described cad expression as being normal in fkh- mutants.
claims.source: Our findings contrast with a previous report, which described cad expression as being normal in fkh- mutants (Jürgens and Weigel, 1988).

claims.claim: Morphogenesis was abnormal in fkh- mutants, in that proctodaeal invagination was delayed until after stage 7.
claims.source: Morphogenesis was abnormal in fkh- mutants, in that proctodaeal invagination was delayed until after stage 7 (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The finding that morphogenesis in fkh- mutants is abnormal contrasts with previous reports that morphogenesis in fkh- mutants is normal until the end of the extended germband stage.
claims.source: This finding contrasts with previous reports that morphogenesis in fkh- mutants is normal until the end of the extended germband stage (Weigel et al., 1989; Wu and Lengyel, 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim contrasts the current findings with previous reports.

claims.claim: cadm-z- mutants show a similar morphogenetic delay to fkh- mutants as well as other defects in posterior invagination.
claims.source: cadm-z- mutants (which have severely reduced fkh expression) show a similar morphogenetic delay (Figure 7—figure supplement 4) as well as other defects in posterior invagination (Wu and Lengyel, 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 and a citation to Wu and Lengyel, 1998.

claims.claim: Posterior invagination is dependent on Fog signalling.
claims.source: Posterior invagination is dependent on Fog signalling (Costa et al., 1994; Sweeton et al., 1991; Parks and Wieschaus, 1991), which is known to be reduced in cadm-z- mutants (Wu and Lengyel, 1998).

claims.claim: Fog signalling is reduced in cadm-z- mutants.
claims.source: Posterior invagination is dependent on Fog signalling (Costa et al., 1994; Sweeton et al., 1991; Parks and Wieschaus, 1991), which is known to be reduced in cadm-z- mutants (Wu and Lengyel, 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu and Lengyel, 1998.

claims.claim: The reduction in Fog signalling in cadm-z- mutants may be mediated by the reduction in Fkh.
claims.source: As Fkh is known to activate Fog signalling in other developmental contexts (Chung et al., 2017), the reduction in Fog signalling may be mediated by the reduction in Fkh.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative and based on a citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claims.claim: A consistent pattern was found across wild-type, cadm-z-, hkb-, and tll- genotypes, in which the fkh border abutted the posterior border of the cad tail domain, and posterior wg was only expressed in fkh-positive hkb-negative territory.
claims.source: We found a consistent pattern across wild-type, cadm-z-, hkb-, and tll- genotypes, in which the fkh border abutted the posterior border of the cad tail domain, and posterior wg was only expressed in fkh-positive hkb-negative territory.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claims.claim: In fkh- mutants, the posterior wg domain was largely lost.
claims.source: Accordingly, in fkh- mutants, the posterior wg domain was largely lost.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claims.claim: Fkh activates wg.
claims.source: These results are consistent with previously proposed regulatory interactions: that Fkh activates wg (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), that Cad activates fkh (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), and that Tll and Hkb indirectly enable fkh to be expressed (Weigel et al., 1990; Casanova, 1990; Goldstein et al., 1999; Morán and Jiménez, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu and Lengyel, 1998 and by data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Cad activates fkh.
claims.source: These results are consistent with previously proposed regulatory interactions: that Fkh activates wg (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), that Cad activates fkh (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), and that Tll and Hkb indirectly enable fkh to be expressed (Weigel et al., 1990; Casanova, 1990; Goldstein et al., 1999; Morán and Jiménez, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu and Lengyel, 1998 and by data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Tll and Hkb indirectly enable fkh to be expressed.
claims.source: These results are consistent with previously proposed regulatory interactions: that Fkh activates wg (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), that Cad activates fkh (Wu and Lengyel, 1998), and that Tll and Hkb indirectly enable fkh to be expressed (Weigel et al., 1990; Casanova, 1990; Goldstein et al., 1999; Morán and Jiménez, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and by data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The activation of wg by Cad appears to be indirect, via Fkh.
claims.source: Accordingly, the activation of wg by Cad (Wu and Lengyel, 1998) appears to be indirect, via Fkh (see Appendix 3—table 1 for detailed reasoning).

claims.source: So, how does timer gene regulation differ between sequentially segmenting embryos (which establish a persistent segment addition zone) and simultaneously segmenting embryos like Drosophila? One key difference is likely to be the role of a posterior Wnt signalling centre: there is evidence from many different sequentially segmenting species that Wnt signalling is important for activating cad expression and maintaining the segment addition zone (reviewed in Clark et al., 2019), whereas we found that timer gene expression was unaffected in Drosophila wg- mutants, at least during our stages of interest.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

results.result: Two parasegment-like boundaries (PSB15 and PSB16) form sequentially in the Drosophila tail region after gastrulation. PSB15 emerges during germband extension (stage 8.1-8.4) with wg14/en15 and slp14/eve15 stripes. PSB16 emerges at the end of germband extension (stage 11.1) with wg15/en16 and slp15/eve16 stripes. Unlike trunk segmentation, these resolved eve stripes appear de novo without a pair-rule phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C24 collectively demonstrate sequential tail segmentation through multiplexed imaging data (Figure 1). The identification of wg15, en16, slp15, and eve16 domains is directly supported by imaging evidence. The temporal sequence and spatial relationships are well-documented, and the contrast with trunk segmentation dynamics is clearly established.

results.result: In the trunk, timer genes (cad, D, opa) are expressed sequentially over stages 4-6 with similar temporal dynamics across the region. Cad clears by stage 5.4, D peaks at stage 5.2 then declines, and Opa appears at stage 5.1 and increases through stage 6. Protein dynamics match transcript dynamics with time-lags for synthesis and decay.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C37 are well-supported by imaging data in Figure 2 and supplementary figures showing both transcript and protein expression. The sequential expression pattern is clearly documented with quantitative expression traces. The correlation between transcript and protein dynamics with appropriate time-lags is demonstrated.

results.result: Timer gene expression in the tail shows the same cad/D/opa sequence as the trunk but is delayed. Cad is expressed continuously through stage 5, while D and opa remain low/absent until late stage 5. High-resolution imaging reveals posterior shifting dynamics with opa transcription gradually invading the cad tail domain from the anterior edge.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C49 are supported by imaging data in Figures 2-3 showing delayed timer gene expression in the tail. The high-resolution close-ups in Figure 3 provide clear evidence for the spatial relationships and posterior shifting dynamics. The correlation with segmentation mode differences is well-established.

results.result: Timer gene mutant analysis reveals cross-regulatory interactions. In opa- mutants, D expression persists longer and the tail domain is stronger. In D- mutants, cad persists abnormally with AP modulation. In cadm-z- mutants, cad persists, D is weaker early, the D tail domain is ventrally restricted, and the posterior wg domain is generally absent.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C66 are well-supported by imaging data in Figure 4 and supplementary figures showing mutant phenotypes. The expression changes in each mutant are clearly documented with both images and quantitative traces. The phenotypic variability and rescue experiments are appropriately characterized.

results.result: Timer gene cross-regulatory interactions inferred from mutant phenotypes: Cad activates D, D represses cad, and Opa represses both D and cad. Additionally, Cad is required for posterior wg expression, D has modest effects on the posterior fate map, and maternal vs. zygotic Cad have distinct roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 represent logical inferences from the mutant phenotype data (Figure 4). The regulatory interactions are well-reasoned based on the observed expression changes. The distinction between maternal and zygotic Cad effects is supported by the rescue experiments. Detailed reasoning is provided in Appendix 3-table 1.

results.result: Tll and hkb are expressed in nested domains at the posterior pole with dynamic spatiotemporal patterns. Tll expression extends further from the pole than hkb, peaks at stage 5.2, and the tll border retracts posteriorly over time. The tll and hkb borders correlate closely with timer gene expression boundaries, with the wg posterior domain emerging at the cad/hkb border.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C89 are well-supported by imaging data in Figure 5 and supplementary figures. The nested expression domains, temporal dynamics, and spatial correlations with timer genes are clearly documented. The posterior retraction of the tll border is quantified and the correlation with timer gene boundaries is evident.

results.result: Terminal system mutant analysis reveals spatial regulation of timer genes. In tor- mutants, all posterior spatial patterning is lost. In tll- mutants, timer gene domains expand posteriorly to abut hkb, and a posteriorly shifted cad tail domain is transiently expressed. In hkb- mutants, the terminal pattern shifts posteriorly and the tll domain is smaller than normal.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C108 are well-supported by imaging data in Figure 6 and supplementary figures. The mutant phenotypes are clearly documented with both images and quantitative traces. The finding of a posteriorly shifted cad tail domain in tll- mutants (C99-C100) contrasts with previous reports but is clearly shown in the data.

results.result: Terminal system genes spatially regulate timer genes: all posterior patterning depends on tor, tll perturbations affect tail/hindgut boundaries, hkb perturbations affect posterior midgut boundaries. Tll strongly represses D and opa and weakly represses cad, while Hkb represses wg, cad, D, and opa. Hkb is necessary for normal tll activation and timely repression.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C116 represent well-reasoned inferences from the terminal mutant phenotype data (Figures 6-7). The regulatory interactions are logically deduced from the observed expression changes. The cross-regulation between hkb and tll is a novel finding supported by the reduced tll domain in hkb- mutants.

results.result: Fkh demarcates the tail/hindgut border and activates posterior wg. The fkh border aligns with the cad tail domain posterior border, and posterior wg is only expressed in fkh-positive hkb-negative territory. In fkh- mutants, the posterior wg domain is largely absent and morphogenesis is abnormal with delayed proctodaeal invagination.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C134 are well-supported by imaging data in Figure 7 and supplementary figures. The spatial relationships between fkh, cad, and wg are clearly documented. The fkh- mutant phenotype and morphogenetic defects are well-characterized. The finding of delayed invagination contrasts with previous reports but is clearly shown.

results.result: Regulatory interactions involving fkh: Fkh activates wg, Cad activates fkh, and Tll and Hkb indirectly enable fkh expression. The activation of wg by Cad appears to be indirect via Fkh.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C138 are supported by the mutant phenotype data in Figure 7 and are consistent with previously proposed interactions. The inference that Cad activates wg indirectly via Fkh is well-reasoned based on the expression patterns and mutant phenotypes.

results.result: A logical model of the inferred regulatory network (11 new interactions) accurately recapitulates wild-type and mutant patterning dynamics. The model explains how graded Tll delineates tail boundaries by differentially repressing timer genes, and how transient Tll expression delays timer gene activation in the tail. Simulated mutants show appropriate spatial transformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C157 are supported by the modeling results in Figure 8. The logical model successfully reproduces the qualitative patterning dynamics observed experimentally. The simulations of wild-type and eight mutant genotypes show good agreement with the data, validating the inferred regulatory network. The model provides mechanistic insights into tail patterning.

results.result: The study demonstrates four main implications: (1) timer gene expression is partially driven by intrinsic network dynamics, (2) cadm-z- embryos precociously express neuroectodermal genes, (3) a coherent model for posterior terminal patterning is produced, and (4) the segmental nature of the Drosophila tail is clarified.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C161 accurately summarize the main findings of the study. Each implication is well-supported by the data presented: C158 by the mutant analysis (Figure 4), C159 by the msh expression data (Figure 4-supplement 3A), C160 by the network model (Figure 8), and C161 by the segmentation data (Figure 1).

results.result: Timer gene cross-regulatory interactions: Cad activates D (promotes next gene), D represses cad and Opa represses cad and D (inhibit previous genes), while opa is not cross-regulated. Tll differentially represses cad, D, and opa in the tail, indirectly maintaining cad expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C165 summarize the key regulatory interactions inferred from the mutant analysis. These are well-supported by the data in Figures 4-6 and represent a coherent model of timer gene regulation. The lack of cross-regulation of opa is an important finding.

results.result: The study identifies 11 new regulatory interactions in Drosophila AP patterning and presents the first formalized model for tail patterning, providing a foundation for future quantitative analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C174 accurately summarize the novelty and significance of the work. The 11 new interactions are documented in Figure 8A and Appendix 3-table 1. The logical model (Figure 8C-K) represents the first formalized model of tail patterning according to the authors' knowledge.

results.result: Tll expression is strong and persistent in the hindgut but weaker and transient in the tail, with the anterior border retracting posteriorly over time. Tll patterns both tail boundaries by differentially repressing D and opa (even at weak levels) relative to cad (only at strong levels). This retraction explains the posterior shifting dynamics of timer genes in the tail.
results.evaluation: Claims C175-C179 are well-supported by the tll expression data (Figure 5) and mutant analysis (Figures 6-7). The differential repression model is inferred from the mutant phenotypes and modeling results (Figure 8). The explanation for posterior shifting dynamics is logical and well-reasoned.

results.result: A concerted posterior fate map shift occurs in hkb- embryos, mediated by reduced tll domain size. A subtle anterior shift may occur in D- embryos. The phenotype implies tll domain size is not an unmediated response to terminal signaling, and hints exist for zygotic cross-regulation of tll and hkb by other AP genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C182 are supported by the hkb- mutant data (Figure 6E-H) showing reduced tll domain and posterior fate map shift. C181 is more speculative but based on data (Figure 4B). C183 is supported by citations to previous work suggesting additional cross-regulation.

results.result: The study presents evidence for a vestigial 16th parasegment boundary in the Drosophila embryo by identifying wg15, en16, slp15, and eve16 domains. This suggests the anal pads are located in PS16/A11, though PSB16 appears dorsoventrally restricted and may have little functional significance.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C189 are supported by the imaging data in Figure 1 and discussion of previous literature. The identification of the additional expression domains is clear, though the functional significance and exact segmental identity remain somewhat uncertain (C189 is appropriately cautious).

results.result: The Drosophila embryo sequentially patterns two parasegment boundaries after gastrulation, both patterned by abutting slp and eve stripes. The relative arrangement of slp, eve, wg, and en is conserved with trunk boundaries and across arthropods, but tail segmentation differs in that eve stripes emerge de novo with single-segmental periodicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C190-C193 are well-supported by the imaging data in Figure 1 and comparative discussion. The sequential patterning, conserved gene arrangement, and distinct mode of eve stripe formation are clearly documented and represent important findings about tail segmentation.

results.result: Timer gene regulation involves both localized terminal system inputs and global temporal regulation by nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio and maternal factors. Timer genes have broad effects on developmental timing, with Opa acting as a pioneer factor and Cad/Cdx playing deeply conserved roles in posterior body formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C172 are supported by the current data and extensive citations to previous work. C167 cites Lu et al. 2009, C168 cites Soluri et al. 2020 and Koromila et al. 2020, C170 is supported by Figure 4-supplement 3A, and C171-C172 cite comparative studies. These represent established knowledge integrated with new findings.

results.result: Similar switches from double-segment to single-segment periodicity occur in other arthropods (Strigamia, Tribolium), hinting that terminal and trunk segments may be homonomous at the segment-polarity level but derived from distinct ontogenetic programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C194-C195 are supported by citations to previous work (Brena and Akam 2013, Janssen 2014). However, C196 is explicitly speculative and requires additional comparative data to be fully supported. The hypothesis is reasonable but remains to be tested.

results.result: Timer gene cross-regulatory interactions may be conserved in insect segmentation. Activation of D by Cad and repression of cad/D by Opa are consistent with segment addition zone organization in Tribolium, though repression of cad by D requires reconciliation. Some interactions may be important in other developmental contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C197-C200 are largely speculative about evolutionary conservation. C198 cites Clark and Peel 2018 for comparison, C199 notes a potential inconsistency, and C200 cites Abdusselamoglu et al. 2019 for a different context. These are reasonable hypotheses but require experimental validation in other species.

results.result: Terminal system components were recruited at different evolutionary times, with posterior tll expression found across holometabolans but not hemipterans, while hkb and tor were recruited more recently. In Tribolium and Nasonia, tor/tll perturbations affect posterior cad expression, potentially via ectopic Opa.
results.evaluation: Claims C201-C204 are supported by citations to comparative studies. However, C205-C206 are explicitly speculative, proposing future experiments to test whether cad loss in other species is mediated by ectopic Opa. This is a reasonable hypothesis but remains untested.

results.result: Timer gene regulation likely differs between sequential and simultaneous segmentation modes in the role of posterior Wnt signaling and timer gene cross-regulation of opa. A modified Drosophila network incorporating Wg activation of Cad and Cad activation of Opa produces appropriate segment addition zone dynamics, suggesting the Drosophila timer gene interactions may be an evolutionary vestige.
results.evaluation: Claims C207-C209 are supported by citations and data (Figure 4-supplement 4). However, C210-C212 are speculative about evolutionary scenarios. The modified model (Figure 8-supplement 1) shows plausible dynamics but the evolutionary hypothesis requires comparative functional experiments to be validated.
